title: Homes Around the World
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: A home is a shelter first of all, and the shape of a traditional house usually tells us about the climate, the materials and the way of life of the people who built it. Across the world, people have invented hundreds of designs, from houses on stilts to homes dug into hillsides, and many are still used today. This passage looks at four traditional homes, each of which has a distinctive roof: a flat-roofed house of mud, a pitched-roof house of wood, a domed shelter of snow and a cone-shaped tent. Each is a clever solution to a problem that people faced in their own environment, and each has lessons for modern architects.

In dry regions, such as the edge of the Sahara, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia, people built houses with thick walls of mud bricks and a flat roof. Mud is cheap and plentiful, and a wall half a metre thick keeps the heat out during the day and holds it in at night, so that the rooms stay comfortable even when the temperature outside changes by twenty degrees. Because rain is rare, there is no need for a sloping roof. The flat roof is a useful extra room, where families dry fruit and sleep on hot summer nights. The weak point is rain: a heavy storm can wash away the mud, and the roof must be repaired every year.

In forested, rainy lands, such as Scandinavia and Japan, people built houses of timber with steep, pitched roofs. A steep roof sheds rain and snow quickly, which prevents the weight of snow from crushing the house. Wood is a good insulator, and a thick roof of thatch, turf or wooden tiles keeps out the cold. Some of these houses are raised on stone or wooden supports, to protect the wood from damp. In Japan, the roofs of old farmhouses are so steep that people call the style praying hands, and the space beneath them was used for raising silkworms.

In the Arctic, the Inuit built temporary winter shelters of snow, called igloos. The builder cut blocks of hard snow with a long knife and laid them in a rising spiral, each block leaning slightly inwards, until the walls met at the top in a dome. A dome is the strongest shape for a roof of blocks, because the weight presses the pieces together. Snow is a better insulator than most people expect, since it is full of trapped air; inside an igloo heated only by a small lamp, the temperature may be close to zero while outside it falls to minus forty. A skilled builder could make an igloo in about an hour.

The nomads of the North American plains lived in tipis, tents shaped like cones. A tipi has a frame of long wooden poles tied together at the top, covered with animal skins, and it has an opening at the top through which the smoke from a fire escapes. The cone is a good shape for wind, because a strong gust slides around it, and when the weather becomes hot, the bottom edge can be lifted for air to pass through. The most important advantage, however, is that a family could take it down in less than half an hour and carry it on horses to follow the herds of buffalo.

In Central Asia, nomads in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Mongolia developed another kind of portable home, the yurt. It has a circular wall of folding wooden lattice, a roof of curved poles meeting in a wheel at the top, and a covering of thick felt made from sheep's wool. The roof is rounded like a low dome. A yurt is warm in the winter, cool in the summer, and so strong that it can withstand fierce steppe winds. It can be taken apart and loaded on to camels or horses in a few hours. Today, many families still keep a yurt for the summer pastures, and tourists stay in them.

Dr Leila Haddad, an architect who studies traditional buildings, says that modern designers have much to learn. Each of these homes uses local materials, requires little energy, and is suited exactly to its climate. Modern glass buildings, by contrast, often need air-conditioning all year round. She does not suggest that people should return to mud and felt, but argues that new houses should borrow the ideas: thick walls in hot countries, steep roofs where snow falls, and materials that can be found nearby. Some builders have already begun to follow her advice, and several new schools in dry regions are built of rammed earth.
